 Telford Vice Share Tweet Bangladesh tour of South Africa, 2026 A tale of two centuries, a near miss, and two dads
 by Telford Vice •     Ackerman and Hamza were involved in a double century partnership. © Getty Ackerman and Hamza were involved in a double century partnership. © Getty Two civilians wandered up the stairs to the Wanderers nets on Saturday. They spotted a short, slight, compact, well-organised cappuccino-coloured South Africa player taking throwdowns. One of the intruders turned to the other and asked: “Marques Ackerman?”
 The other looked over the speaker’s shoulder at Ackerman sitting padded up several metres away. The man batting was a different short, slight, compact, well-organised cappuccino-coloured South Africa player: Zubayr Hamza.
 It shouldn’t be difficult to confuse them: Ackerman bats left-handed, Hamza not. Even more starkly, to South Africans, they are not of the same race. How could you get that wrong?
 Yet you only had to watch them bat together on Monday to understand. They were of one mind and one approach, albeit Ackerman naturally is the more attacking batter. He took risks early on, but settled into a Hamzaesque groove soon enough.
 Together they got on top of a flattening pitch and a flaccid Bangladesh attack — the feisty Hasan Mahmud excepted — to share a stand of 202. It was a remarkable effort considering Ackerman and Hamza had batted together in a first-class match just once before. But they also did so profitably then, putting on 170 for South Africa A against their Bangladesh counterparts in Pretoria in August. How, given they are relative strangers, were they able to communicate so smoothly?
 “Our relationship is really good,” Ackerman told a press conference. “It was really good to see him come into the space and to bat with him and for us to motivate each other to keep going. We understand each other’s game.”
 The partnership helped take South Africa to within 113 runs of parity with the visitors’ first innings of 400; the highest made by any Asian team in the opening innings of a series in this country.
 How many more the home side might score on the third day, usually the best for batting here, with Temba Bavuma and Ryan Rickelton at the crease and Wiaan Mulder, Marco Jansen and Simon Harmer to come — and with at least 18 overs to come before the bowlers get their hands on a new ball — is an ominous thought.
 But let’s not get ahead of ourselves. When Ackerman reached 95 against Australia at Newlands last month he faced three deliveries without scoring, lurched down the pitch to the fourth, and was easily stumped off Nathan Lyon. This time, having made it to 94, he showed no such rashness and took nine balls to secure his first Test century in his fourth innings. He needed a single when Taskin Ahmed served up a shoulder-high bouncer, which was deftly angled to fine leg.
 There was probably two in it, but Ackerman was too busy leaping and punching the syrupy afternoon air to bother turning for a second run. He and Hamza shared an embrace once the fuss was over.
 C’mon Zuby. Your turn. Hamza also looked locked and loaded for a century, but 21 balls after Ackerman reached his ton he stretched far forward to Mominul Haque. Too far forward — the ball bit and turned and took the edge and lodged in Litton Das’ gloves.
 Hamza turned in the direction of the walk he knew he had to take, but somehow he couldn’t manage the first step. He stood at the crease for what felt like a week, maybe thinking about his long, hard road back into a line-up he has been part of only four times in more than the past four years, maybe wondering what might have been had he not been suspended for nine months in 2022 after testing positive for a banned substance, maybe trying to convince himself that 83 was as good as a hundred.
 He set off finally, but did not raise his bat until he was a step or three from crossing the boundary. No sooner was his bat up than he whipped it down in unvarnished anger. The pain of those 17 unscored runs ran deep. As Ackerman said, “He deserved a ton out there today.”
 Ackerman forged on in ever more strident fashion; charging Mehidy Hasan and edging the resultant full toss for four, doing so again and putting the off-spinner over cover for another boundary, pulling Mominul flat and furious for four, pulling Mehidy for another in the air, and another through midwicket, and still another smoked through cover, mistiming a hoik off Mominul that streaked to the midwicket fence nonetheless, and launching him properly deep into the shadows of the grass bank beyond midwicket.
 “We want Ebadot!” wobbled the chant from a steadily more beered-up throng of South Africa fans near the long-on boundary at the Corlett Drive End. Fat chance of that. Ebadot Hossain, then Bangladesh’s most expensive bowler, sent down his last delivery to Ackerman when the left-hander was still a dozen runs shy of his century.
 He had made it all the way to 157 when he raced down the pitch to Mahmud, went on the hook and sent a catch spiralling to deep backward square. The end of his innings felt like the dousing of a vast fire.
 Ackerman’s wife Tess and their young son Jack were among other family members at the ground to celebrate with him. Not so Litton Das’ nearest and dearest, who it is to be hoped were watching from afar when he turned his overnight 92 into his seventh century.
 On reaching the milestone, with a top-edged pull off Marco Jansen that flew over fine leg for six, Litton fished a note out of his pocket. It read: “Happy birthday my princess”. Litton and his wife Devashri Biswas Sonchita have a daughter, Anayra, who turned three on Monday.
 “Whenever I talk to her when I’m playing she says, ‘Papa, I need a century from you.’,” Litton told a press conference. “So this century is for her.”
 But the note took some planning. And confidence that he would reach three figures. What if he hadn’t?
 “That’s what hope does,” Litton said. “When you think about the future, you think positive things. If I didn’t score a century the note would still be in my pocket.”
 Litton said he devised his plan on Monday morning: “I was thinking how to surprise her.”
 Problem: Litton didn’t trust his handwriting to be legible enough. So he leant on the team’s media manager, Abu Noman Amit, to do the needful.
 Jack Ackerman’s second birthday isn’t until January. But did his father think about following Litton’s lead anyway?
 “No, nothing fancy like that,” Ackerman said. “It’s not only about when you do well. It’s also when you don't do well, and you have your family there and people backing you up and keeping you sane.”
 Litton didn’t have that. But he had something else. As he walked into the room for his presser he passed an air-hockey table. Without breaking stride Litton grabbed one of the paddles and struck the puck solidly. It streaked straight and true into the goal at the other end of the table.
 Doubtless that too was for little Anayra so far away.
